questions.questionText: Which tourism sector includes hotels and guesthouses?
questions.explanation: Hotels and guesthouses provide overnight lodging and belong to the accommodation sector.

curriculum.objective: Explain tourism-sector relationships and use visitor motivation to interpret demand and product choices.

questions.questionText: A visitor travels mainly to relax on a beach and escape work pressure. What is the primary motivation?
questions.explanation: Relaxation and escape are leisure motivations rather than business, study or visiting-friends-and-relatives travel.

curriculum.objective: Explain tourism-sector relationships and use visitor motivation to interpret demand and product choices.

questions.questionText: Which example best shows interdependence in tourism?
options: A museum changes its logo colour
An airline delay disrupts transfers and hotel check-in
questions.correctAnswer: An airline delay disrupts transfers and hotel check-in
questions.explanation: Transport, transfers and accommodation form a connected chain, so failure in one sector affects the others.

curriculum.objective: Explain tourism-sector relationships and use visitor motivation to interpret demand and product choices.

questions.questionText: Which condition most reduces a destination’s tourism multiplier effect?
options: Hotels importing most supplies and sending profits abroad
questions.correctAnswer: Hotels importing most supplies and sending profits abroad
questions.explanation: Imports and externally transferred profits create leakage, so less visitor spending recirculates through the local economy.

curriculum.objective: Explain tourism-sector relationships and use visitor motivation to interpret demand and product choices.

questions.questionText: What is destination carrying capacity?
options: The number of aircraft using an airport
The visitor level supportable without unacceptable damage or experience decline
The maximum price tourists will pay
The number of hotels owned locally
questions.correctAnswer: The visitor level supportable without unacceptable damage or experience decline
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity concerns the amount and type of use a destination can support before environmental, social or visitor-quality limits are exceeded.

curriculum.objective: Analyse carrying capacity, seasonality, lifecycle position and tourism impacts when evaluating destination decisions.

questions.questionText: Which is a likely positive economic impact of tourism?
options: Guaranteed equal income for all residents
Creation of jobs and income in connected local businesses
questions.correctAnswer: Creation of jobs and income in connected local businesses
questions.explanation: Visitor spending can support direct and indirect employment and income across accommodation, food, transport and suppliers.

curriculum.objective: Analyse carrying capacity, seasonality, lifecycle position and tourism impacts when evaluating destination decisions.

questions.questionText: Why can strong seasonality be difficult for a tourism business?
options: Every visitor spends the same amount
Fixed costs disappear in low season
Revenue and staffing needs fluctuate sharply across the year
questions.correctAnswer: Revenue and staffing needs fluctuate sharply across the year
questions.explanation: Seasonal peaks and troughs create unstable cash flow, capacity use and employment needs while many fixed costs continue.

curriculum.objective: Analyse carrying capacity, seasonality, lifecycle position and tourism impacts when evaluating destination decisions.

questions.questionText: A mature destination has falling repeat visits and outdated attractions. Which response best supports responsible renewal?
options: Diversify products and upgrade them using resident and environmental input
Remove all local businesses from the centre
questions.correctAnswer: Diversify products and upgrade them using resident and environmental input
questions.explanation: Responsible rejuvenation refreshes appeal while involving residents and managing environmental and social constraints.

curriculum.objective: Analyse carrying capacity, seasonality, lifecycle position and tourism impacts when evaluating destination decisions.

questions.questionText: Which facility most directly improves access for a visitor using a wheelchair?
options: Advertising videos with decorative captions only
questions.explanation: Step-free movement and accessible facilities remove physical barriers and support independent use of the destination.

curriculum.objective: Apply inclusive communication and service-recovery principles to meet visitor needs and resolve service failures.

questions.questionText: What is the best first response to a reasonable customer complaint?
options: Explain immediately why the customer is wrong
Listen, acknowledge the problem and clarify the desired resolution
questions.correctAnswer: Listen, acknowledge the problem and clarify the desired resolution
questions.explanation: Active listening and clarification show respect, establish facts and allow a proportionate solution.

curriculum.objective: Apply inclusive communication and service-recovery principles to meet visitor needs and resolve service failures.

questions.questionText: Which communication approach is most suitable for visitors with varied language backgrounds?
options: Use plain language, avoid idioms and confirm understanding
Speak faster and more loudly in every case
questions.correctAnswer: Use plain language, avoid idioms and confirm understanding
questions.explanation: Clear wording, reduced idiom and a respectful understanding check lower avoidable language barriers.

curriculum.objective: Apply inclusive communication and service-recovery principles to meet visitor needs and resolve service failures.

questions.questionText: A family’s booked excursion is cancelled at short notice. Which service recovery is strongest?
options: Offer a suitable alternative or refund promptly, then confirm the arrangement
Give the same solution without checking family needs
questions.correctAnswer: Offer a suitable alternative or refund promptly, then confirm the arrangement
questions.explanation: Prompt choice, clear confirmation and a remedy matched to the family’s needs address both practical loss and trust.

curriculum.objective: Apply inclusive communication and service-recovery principles to meet visitor needs and resolve service failures.

questions.questionText: Grouping potential visitors by age, income and family stage is which type of segmentation?
questions.explanation: Age, income and family lifecycle are demographic characteristics used to define market segments.

curriculum.objective: Use segmentation, primary research, product lifecycle and the marketing mix to support tourism decisions.

questions.questionText: Which activity produces primary market research?
questions.explanation: A survey conducted for the current decision gathers new first-hand data and is therefore primary research.

curriculum.objective: Use segmentation, primary research, product lifecycle and the marketing mix to support tourism decisions.

questions.questionText: What usually characterises the growth stage of a tourism product lifecycle?
options: Sales collapse and the product leaves the market
Sales rise and competitors begin entering
No customer knows the product exists
questions.correctAnswer: Sales rise and competitors begin entering
questions.explanation: During growth, awareness and sales increase, often attracting competitors and requiring expansion or differentiation.

curriculum.objective: Use segmentation, primary research, product lifecycle and the marketing mix to support tourism decisions.

questions.questionText: Which plan best applies the marketing mix to a budget adventure segment?
options: Luxury pricing with no online information
One identical message for every traveller
An affordable activity bundle sold through mobile channels with targeted promotion
A high price unrelated to product features
questions.correctAnswer: An affordable activity bundle sold through mobile channels with targeted promotion
questions.explanation: The product, price, distribution and promotion are aligned with the segment’s budget, activity interest and booking behaviour.

curriculum.objective: Use segmentation, primary research, product lifecycle and the marketing mix to support tourism decisions.

questions.questionText: What is essential in a workable multi-stop itinerary?
options: Realistic travel times and a logical visit sequence
The maximum possible number of stops
questions.correctAnswer: Realistic travel times and a logical visit sequence
questions.explanation: A feasible itinerary accounts for routing, travel duration, opening times and human needs rather than only listing attractions.

curriculum.objective: Calculate and plan feasible tourism operations using itineraries, capacity, contingency and commercial information.

questions.questionText: A coach has 200 seats and carries 150 passengers. What is its passenger load factor?
questions.explanation: Load factor = occupied capacity ÷ available capacity × 100 = 150 ÷ 200 × 100 = 75%.

curriculum.objective: Calculate and plan feasible tourism operations using itineraries, capacity, contingency and commercial information.

questions.questionText: An outdoor heritage walk may be cancelled by severe weather. What is the strongest contingency?
options: Tell visitors only after the scheduled start
Pre-arrange an indoor alternative and a clear notification process
questions.correctAnswer: Pre-arrange an indoor alternative and a clear notification process
questions.explanation: A safe alternative plus timely communication preserves value and reduces confusion when the primary activity cannot operate.

curriculum.objective: Calculate and plan feasible tourism operations using itineraries, capacity, contingency and commercial information.

questions.questionText: A package costs $800 to provide. What selling price gives a 25% markup on cost?
questions.explanation: A 25% markup is 0.25 × 800 = $200, so selling price is $800 + $200 = $1,000.

curriculum.objective: Calculate and plan feasible tourism operations using itineraries, capacity, contingency and commercial information.
